docs.title: Documentation deploy
docs.text:
To build the documentation, mkdocs creates a new folder site/ which contains all the HTML, CSS and JS files that are created with the build command. To deploy this documentation in git, I created a new github pages instance, which points to gh-pages git branch. This git branch contains the site/ files.

%%{init: {'logLevel': 'debug', 'theme': 'neutral', 'gitGraph': {'showBranches': true, 'showCommitLabel': true}}}%%
    gitGraph
      commit id: "a"
      commit id: "docs folder" type: HIGHLIGHT
      branch gh-pages
      checkout gh-pages
      commit id: "update site folder"
      checkout main
      commit id: "c"

After the commit in the docs/ main folder, a Github Actions workflow is triggered in which:

  1. Requirements are installed;
  2. Command mkdocs gh-deploy runs and updates the gh-pages branch with the site/ folder.
pages-deploy.yml
name: build and deploy - mkdocs
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths:
      - 'docs/**'
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v2
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v2
        with:
          python-version: 3.x
      - run: |
          cd docs
          pip install -r requirements.txt
          mkdocs gh-deploy --force --clean --verbose

Afterwards, the documentation site https://joaohb07.github.io/documentation is updated by gh-pages branch.

docs.title: M/M/s Queueing System Simulator
docs.text:
Stochastic Modeling & Native OOXML Reporting

A zero-dependency discrete-event stochastic queueing simulator written in Python for evaluating single-queue, multi-server (\(M/M/s\)) service systems. Developed for the Modeling and Evaluation of Computer Systems (Modelagem e Avaliação de Sistemas Computacionais) course at São Paulo State University (UNESP), the project implements a multiplicative Park–Miller pseudo-random number generator (PRNG), inverse transform exponential variate sampling, earliest-available parallel server routing, and a native .xlsx spreadsheet exporter built directly over the Office Open XML (ECMA-376) specification.

docs.text:

docs.title: System Architecture & Simulation Pipeline
docs.text:
The simulator is decoupled into three pure-Python modules with zero third-party dependencies (relying strictly on math, zipfile, pathlib, and xml.sax.saxutils), separating stochastic variate generation, discrete-event server scheduling, and binary Office Open XML packaging:

flowchart TD
    CLI["🖥️ CLI Driver<br/>(main.py)<br/>Seeds, Server Count s, List Size"] --> PRNG["🎲 Park–Miller LCG<br/>(generate_random_numbers)<br/>xₙ₊₁ = (16807·xₙ) mod (2³¹−1)"]
    PRNG -->|"Dual Independent Streams<br/>U₁ (Arrivals), U₂ (Service)"| InvTrans["📈 Inverse Transform Sampling<br/>(generate_inputs_until_time)<br/>TEC = −ln(U₁)/λ, TS = −ln(U₂)/μ"]
    InvTrans -->|"Bounded Horizon<br/>t_arrival ≤ T_max (300)"| Engine["⚙️ M/M/s Discrete-Event Engine<br/>(simulate_mm_s)<br/>FCFS Queue + Earliest-Free Server"]
    Engine -->|"Per-Customer Telemetry<br/>& Idle Time Matrix"| OOXML["📊 Native OOXML Exporter<br/>(exportador_planilha.py)<br/>ZIP + XML (ECMA-376)"]
    OOXML --> XLSX["📑 Styled Workbook<br/>(planilhas/simulador_MADSC_mms.xlsx)"]

docs.title: Core Engineering Invariants
docs.text:
1. Stream Independence via Dual Seeds: Inter-arrival times (TEC) and service durations (TS) are driven by two decoupled PRNG streams (seed_1 and seed_2), preventing cross-correlation between customer arrival bursts and workload service demands.
  2. Deterministic Replayability: Because the Park–Miller generator is deterministic for a fixed seed pair \((x_0^{(1)}, x_0^{(2)})\), multi-server capacity scaling experiments (\(s \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\)) execute against the exact same arrival and service workload trace.
  3. Zero-Dependency Office Open XML Generation: Rather than relying on heavy external libraries (pandas, openpyxl, or xlsxwriter), the reporting layer constructs the internal ZIP archive structure and XML relationships required by ISO/IEC 29500 ([Content_Types].xml, _rels/.rels, workbook.xml, styles.xml, and sheet1.xml).

docs.title: 1. Kendall's Notation (\(M/M/s/\infty/\text{FCFS}\))
docs.text:
The simulated system models a single-queue, multi-server Markovian facility characterized by:

  • Arrival Process (\(M\) — Markovian / Poisson): Customer arrivals follow a homogeneous Poisson process with arrival rate \(\lambda = 0.5\text{ customers / time unit}\), yielding exponentially distributed inter-arrival times (\(\text{TEC}\)) with mean:
\[ E[\text{TEC}] = \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{1}{0.5} = 2.0\text{ time units} \]
  • Service Process (\(M\) — Exponential): Each of the \(s\) identical parallel servers processes customers with service rate \(\mu = 0.125\text{ customers / time unit}\), yielding exponentially distributed service times (\(\text{TS}\)) with mean:
\[ E[\text{TS}] = \frac{1}{\mu} = \frac{1}{0.125} = 8.0\text{ time units} \]
  • Parallel Servers (\(s\)): Configurable number of homogeneous servers (\(s \ge 1\)) fed by a single First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) queue with infinite buffer capacity.

docs.title: 2. Traffic Intensity & Theoretical Stability Criterion
docs.text:
Under steady-state queueing theory, offered load \(a\) and per-server utilization factor \(\rho\) are governed by:

\[ a = \frac{\lambda}{\mu} = \frac{0.5}{0.125} = 4.0\text{ Erlangs}, \qquad \rho = \frac{\lambda}{s \cdot \mu} = \frac{4.0}{s} \] Configuration Servers (\(s\)) Traffic Intensity (\(\rho = \frac{\lambda}{s\mu}\)) Analytical Regime (\(T \to \infty\)) Finite-Horizon Simulation (\(T_{\max} = 300\)) \(M/M/1\) \(1\) \(\rho = 4.00 > 1\) Unstable (Queue diverges) Server saturated (\(\approx 0\%\) idle); waiting time grows monotonically \(M/M/2\) \(2\) \(\rho = 2.00 > 1\) Unstable (Overloaded) Severe queue buildup; servers remain continuously busy \(M/M/3\) \(3\) \(\rho = 1.33 > 1\) Unstable (Overloaded) Moderate backlog accumulation across simulation horizon \(M/M/4\) \(4\) \(\rho = 1.00\) Critically Loaded Near-equilibrium capacity (\(s\mu = \lambda = 0.5\)) \(M/M/5+\) \(\ge 5\) \(\rho \le 0.80 < 1\) Ergodic Steady State Bounded queue lengths and measurable inter-arrival server idleness

docs.title: 1. Park–Miller Minimal Standard LCG (generate_random_numbers)
docs.text:
Uniform pseudo-random variates \(U_i \in (0, 1)\) are generated via the multiplicative Lehmer / Park–Miller Linear Congruential Generator:

\[ x_{i+1} = (a \cdot x_i + c) \bmod M, \qquad U_i = \frac{x_i}{M} \]

with prime modulus and primitive root parameters:

\[ a = 16807 = 7^5, \qquad c = 0, \qquad M = 2^{31} - 1 = 2\,147\,483\,647 \]

This parametrization guarantees a full maximal period of \(M - 1 = 2^{31} - 2\) non-zero states before sequence repetition. Sequence indexing starts at offset list_position = 2 to maintain exact numerical parity with analytical hand-calculation benchmarks.

docs.title: 2. Inverse Transform Sampling (generate_inputs_until_time)
docs.text:
To map uniform variates \(U \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)\) onto an exponential cumulative distribution function \(F(x) = 1 - e^{-\alpha x}\) (\(\alpha \in \{\lambda, \mu\}\)), the simulator applies the inverse CDF transformation \(X = F^{-1}(U)\):

\[ \text{TEC}_i = -\frac{\ln(U_i^{(1)})}{\lambda} = -\frac{\ln(U_i^{(1)})}{0.5}, \qquad \text{TS}_i = -\frac{\ln(U_i^{(2)})}{\mu} = -\frac{\ln(U_i^{(2)})}{0.125} \]

Arrival timestamps \(A_i\) accumulate sequentially until the simulation horizon \(T_{\max} = 300\) is exceeded (\(A_i > T_{\max}\)), at which point arrival generation terminates cleanly.

docs.title: Discrete-Event Scheduling & Metrics Formulation (simulate_mm_s)
docs.text:
For each customer \(i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) arriving at clock time \(A_i\) with service duration \(\text{TS}_i\):

  1. Earliest-Available Server Selection (Tie-Breaking Rule): Let \(F_k\) denote the timestamp when server \(k \in \{1, \dots, s\}\) completes its currently assigned job (initialized to \(F_k = 0\)). Customer \(i\) is routed to server \(k^*\):

$$ k^* = \arg\min_{k \in {1, \dots, s}} F_k $$

Python's min(range(server_count), key=...) preserves index ordering, deterministically breaking ties in favor of the lowest-numbered server ID.

  1. Service Window & Customer Latency Metrics:

$$ \begin{aligned} T_{\text{start}, i} &= \max(A_i, F_{k^*}) \ T_{\text{end}, i} &= T_{\text{start}, i} + \text{TS}i \ W \ W_i &= T_{\text{end}, i} - A_i \quad \text{(Total Sojourn / System Time)} \end{aligned} $$} &= T_{\text{start}, i} - A_i \quad \text{(Queue Waiting Time)

  1. Per-Server & Horizon-Bounded Idle Time Accounting:
  2. Pre-Service Idle Gap: When \(A_i > F_{k^*}\), server \(k^*\) accumulates idle time \(I_{i, k^*} = \max(0, A_i - F_{k^*})\), recorded both in the sparse customer-by-server idle matrix and in the server's cumulative accumulator.
  3. Post-Completion Residual Idleness: Once all \(N\) arrivals have been scheduled, any remaining idle interval between each server's final service completion \(F_k\) and the simulation horizon \(T_{\max} = 300\) is added:

$$ I_{\text{final}, k} = \max(0, T_{\max} - F_k), \qquad I_{\text{total}, k} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} I_{i, k} + I_{\text{final}, k} $$

docs.title: Native Office Open XML (.xlsx) Exporter (exportador_planilha.py)
docs.text:
Instead of introducing external spreadsheet dependencies, export_spreadsheet() synthesizes a compliant ECMA-376 / ISO-29500 .xlsx package from scratch using Python's zipfile module:

planilhas/simulador_MADSC_mms.xlsx (ZIP Archive)
├── [Content_Types].xml          # MIME type overrides for workbook, worksheet, and stylesheet parts
├── _rels/.rels                  # Root package relationship pointing to xl/workbook.xml
└── xl/
    ├── workbook.xml             # Defines the "Simulador" worksheet entry
    ├── styles.xml               # Custom 5-decimal format (numFmtId="164": 0.00000), fonts, fills & borders
    ├── _rels/workbook.xml.rels  # Links workbook to worksheets/sheet1.xml and styles.xml
    └── worksheets/sheet1.xml    # Sparse cell grid (<c r="C2" s="3"><v>...</v></c>) + summary averages row

docs.title: Spreadsheet Schema & Dynamic Column Expansion
docs.text:
• Columns A–J (Fixed Customer Telemetry): Customer Index, Assigned Server ID, TEC, TS, Arrival Clock Time, Service Start, Service End, Queue Wait Time (\(W_q\)), System Time (\(W\)), and Active Server Idle Time.
  • Columns K–K+s-1 (Dynamic Server Idle Matrix): Dynamically expands to \(s\) columns (Tempo ocioso Servidor 1 .. Tempo ocioso Servidor s), mapping each customer's idle gap to the exact server column and appending a styled summary row (Média) at row client_size + 3.

docs.title: MyPas Compiler
docs.text:
Recursive Descent LL(1) Pascal Compiler

MyPas is a modular, single-pass compiler front-end written in C for a statically typed subset of the Pascal programming language. Developed for the Compilers course at São Paulo State University (UNESP) under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Eraldo Pereira Marinho, the project implements lexical scanning via deterministic finite automata (DFA), predictive top-down \(\text{LL}(1)\) recursive descent parsing, and syntax-directed semantic validation backed by a block-structured symbol table with static lexical scoping (lexlevel).

docs.title: Quick Links
docs.text:
• Source Code Repository: github.com/joaohb07/mypas
  • Authors: João Henrique Botelho, Cristian Santos de Castro, João Pedro Brum Terra
  • Course & Institution: Compilers (2024) — UNESP (Prof. Dr. Eraldo Pereira Marinho)

docs.title: System Architecture & Compilation Pipeline
docs.text:
Unlike multi-pass compilers that materialize an intermediate Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) before performing name and type resolution, MyPas operates as a single-pass, syntax-directed translation (SDT) front-end. Semantic actions—symbol insertion, duplicate detection, lexical visibility lookup, and scope-frame reclamation—are embedded directly within the mutually recursive grammar procedures.

flowchart LR
    Source["📄 Source File<br/>(program.pas)"] --> Stream["🎞️ Character Tape<br/>(FILE* + ungetc)"]
    Stream --> Lexer["🔍 Lexical Analyzer<br/>(lexer.c & keywords.c)<br/>DFA + 1-Char Lookahead"]
    Lexer -->|"Token Stream<br/>⟨token_id, lexeme, ln, col⟩"| Parser["🌳 LL(1) Recursive Parser<br/>(parser.c)<br/>Predictive Top-Down"]
    Parser <-->|"SDT Actions<br/>Lookup / Append / Pop"| SymTab[("🗂️ Symbol Table<br/>(symtab.c)<br/>Static Lexical Scoping")]
    Parser -->|"Scope Trace"| Output["📊 Symbol Table Snapshots<br/>(stdout)"]
    Lexer -.->|"Lexical Fault"| Stderr["🚨 Positional Diagnostics<br/>(stderr: ln, col)"]
    Parser -.->|"Syntax / Scope Fault"| Stderr

docs.title: Core Architectural Invariants
docs.text:
1. Zero-Dependency C Implementation: Built strictly on the C Standard Library (<stdio.h>, <stdlib.h>, <string.h>, <ctype.h>) without external lexer or parser generators (lex/flex or yacc/bison).
  2. Deterministic Single-Token Lookahead (\(k = 1\)): A global lookahead register holds the current unconsumed terminal returned by gettoken(source). Every non-terminal procedure inspects lookahead to select a unique production rule in \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) time with zero backtracking.
  3. Synchronized Source-Coordinate Tracking: The lexical scanner maintains global linenum and colnum state across whitespace, tab stops (+4 columns), and multi-line comments, enabling exact (ln, col) fault reporting across all compilation phases.

docs.title: Formal Language Theory Foundations
docs.text: The front-end design directly maps each compilation phase to its corresponding formal language class in the Chomsky Hierarchy:

docs.title: 1. Lexical Layer — Chomsky Type-3 (Regular Languages)
docs.text:
Implemented across lexer.c and keywords.c, the scanner simulates a Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) over an input character tape (FILE *) augmented with single-character rollback (ungetc()).

  • Whitespace & Comment Filtering (skipspaces): Consumes spaces, tabs, newlines (linenum++, colnum = 1), and block comments delimited by { ... } or (* ... *). Reaching EOF inside an unclosed comment triggers a fatal UNTERMINED_COMMENT_ERROR reporting the opening line.
  • Maximal-Munch Identifiers & Case-Insensitive Keywords (isID & iskeyword): $\(\text{ID} = [A\text{-}Za\text{-}z][A\text{-}Za\text{-}z0\text{-}9]^{*}, \quad |\text{lexeme}| \le \text{MAXIDLEN}\;(32)\)$ Identifiers are scanned greedily until the first non-alphanumeric character (pushed back via ungetc). Because Pascal is case-insensitive, iskeyword() normalizes a local buffer (char identifier[MAXIDLEN + 1]) to lowercase via tolower() and checks the reserved keyword table (BEGIN through END), promoting matching lexemes from generic ID tokens to keyword token codes while preserving original casing for symbol table diagnostics.
  • Multi-Character Operators & Numeric Literals:
  • isASGN disambiguates the assignment operator := (ASGN) from standalone declaration colons :.
  • isRELOP resolves single- and two-character relational operators (=, <>, <=, >=, <, >), rolling back the second character when a single-character < or > is matched.
  • isNUM recognizes integer and floating-point numeric constants ([0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?([eE][+-]?[0-9]+)?).

docs.title: 2. Syntactic Layer — Chomsky Type-2 (\(\text{LL}(1)\) Context-Free Grammar)
docs.text: Implemented in parser.c, the syntactic analyzer is structured as a set of mutually recursive procedures—one per non-terminal—operating on a left-factored, non-left-recursive \(\text{LL}(1)\) grammar.

docs.title: Extended Backus–Naur Form (EBNF) Specification
docs.text:
program   ::= "PROGRAM" ID "(" idlist ")" ";" block "." ;

block     ::= vardef sbprgdef beginend ;

vardef    ::= [ "VAR" idlist ":" type ";" { idlist ":" type ";" } ] ;

sbprgdef  ::= { ( "PROCEDURE" | "FUNCTION" ) ID parmlist [ ":" type ] ";" block ";" } ;

parmlist  ::= [ "(" [ "VAR" ] idlist ":" type { ";" [ "VAR" ] idlist ":" type } ")" ] ;

beginend  ::= "BEGIN" stmtlst "END" ;

stmtlst   ::= stmt { ";" stmt } ;

stmt      ::= idstmt
            | beginend
            | ifstmt
            | whlstmt
            | repstmt
            | ε ;

idstmt    ::= ID [ ":=" expr | "(" exprlist ")" ] ;

ifstmt    ::= "IF" expr "THEN" stmt [ "ELSE" stmt ] ;

whlstmt   ::= "WHILE" expr "DO" stmt ;

repstmt   ::= "REPEAT" stmtlst "UNTIL" expr ;

exprlist  ::= expr { "," expr } ;

expr      ::= smpexpr [ relop smpexpr ] ;

smpexpr   ::= [ "+" | "-" ] term { ( "+" | "-" ) term } ;

term      ::= factor { ( "*" | "/" ) factor } ;

factor    ::= ID [ "(" exprlist ")" ]
            | NUM
            | "(" expr ")" ;

relop     ::= "=" | "<>" | "<=" | ">=" | "<" | ">" ;

type      ::= "INTEGER" | "LONG" | "REAL" | "DOUBLE" | "BOOLEAN" ;

docs.title: Operator Precedence & Associativity Hierarchy
docs.text:
Operator precedence and left-associativity are encoded directly into the recursive non-terminal call chain rather than an external operator-precedence table:

Precedence Non-Terminal Operators / Constructs Associativity 1 (Lowest) expr =, <>, <=, >=, <, > Non-associative 2 smpexpr Unary +, - and binary +, - Left-associative (while loop) 3 term *, / Left-associative (while loop) 4 (Highest) factor Parenthesized ( expr ), function calls ID(...), literals NUM Atomic
  • Predictive Token Matching (match): Verifies lookahead == expected and advances the scanner via lookahead = gettoken(source). On mismatch, it emits SYNTAX_ERROR with the offending lexeme, linenum, and colnum, halting execution immediately (exit(-3)).
  • Dangling-Else Disambiguation: In ifstmt(), the optional if (lookahead == ELSE) branch eagerly binds to the innermost unmatched IF statement, matching standard Pascal semantics.

docs.title: Symbol Table & Static Lexical Scoping (symtab.c)
docs.text: To support arbitrarily nested PROCEDURE and FUNCTION declarations, MyPas manages a contiguous stack-allocated symbol table (SYMTAB symtab[MAXSTBSIZE]) indexed by a stack pointer symtab_next_entry.

docs.title: Symbol Descriptor Structure (SYMTAB)
docs.text:
typedef struct _symtab_ {
    char name[MAXIDLEN + 1]; // Original identifier lexeme (up to 32 chars + NUL)
    int  lexlevel;           // Static nesting depth (1 = global, 2+ = nested subprograms)
    int  objtype;            // 0 = OBJ_PROCEDURE, 1 = OBJ_FUNCTION, 2 = OBJ_VAR
    int  parmflag;           // 1 = formal/program parameter, 0 = local/global variable
    int  type;               // 0 = INT32, 1 = INT64, 2 = FLOAT32, 3 = FLOAT64, 4 = BOOL, 5 = TEXT
} SYMTAB;

docs.title: Lexical Level Lifecycle & \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) Frame Reclamation
docs.text:
1. Global Scope (lexlevel = 1):
  2. Program header arguments (e.g., input, output) are registered at lexlevel = 1 with objtype = OBJ_VAR, parmflag = 1, and type = TEXT.
  3. Top-level VAR declarations and subprogram headers are appended at lexlevel = 1.
  4. Subprogram Entry (lexlevel \(\rightarrow\) lexlevel + 1):
  5. Inside sbprgdef(), the subprogram's own identifier is inserted at the enclosing lexlevel (so outer callers can invoke it) and its index is recorded in first_func_pro_index.
  6. Immediately after match(ID), lexlevel is incremented (lexlevel++) prior to parsing parmlist(), ensuring formal parameters and local variables bind to the inner scope (lexlevel + 1).
  7. Subprogram Exit & Stack Teardown:
  8. After parsing the subprogram's block() and trailing ;, symtab_print() outputs a snapshot of the active symbol table.
  9. All formal parameters and local declarations belonging to the exiting subprogram are popped in \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) time by resetting the stack pointer and decrementing the lexical depth: 
    symtab_next_entry = first_func_pro_index + 1;
lexlevel--;

docs.title: Visibility & Lookup Semantics (symtab_lookup)
docs.text:
• Lexical Visibility Rule: When resolving an identifier in idstmt() or factor(), symtab_lookup(lexeme, lexlevel) permits access to variables declared in the current or any enclosing lexical scope (symtab[i].lexlevel <= lexlevel), as well as visible procedures and functions. Undeclared references trigger SYMBOL_NOT_FOUND_ERROR.
  • Duplicate Detection: symtab_append() checks for existing collisions before inserting a new symbol, reporting SYMBOL_ALREADY_DEFINED_ERROR and incrementing error_count on redeclaration.

docs.title: Repository Structure & Module Breakdown
docs.text:
mypas/
├── constants.h                 # Architectural limits (MAXIDLEN = 32) & error format strings
├── keywords.h / keywords.c     # Reserved keyword table & case-insensitive lookup
├── lexer.h / lexer.c           # DFA scanner, comment stripper, and (ln, col) tracker
├── parser.h / parser.c         # Predictive LL(1) recursive descent parser & SDT actions
├── symtab.h / symtab.c         # Block-structured symbol table & lexical scope lookup
├── mypas.c                     # CLI driver, argument/file validation, and entry point
├── Makefile                    # GNU Make build automation (CFLAGS = -I. -g)
└── inputs/                     # Regression suite of valid and faulty .pas programs
Module Primary Responsibility & Key Functions mypas.c Validates CLI arguments (argc == 2) and .pas extension, opens FILE *source with error checking, primes lookahead = gettoken(source), invokes program(), and prints symtab final. constants.h Defines MAXIDLEN (32), stack/table capacities, and diagnostic message templates (SYNTAX_ERROR, SYMBOL_NOT_FOUND_ERROR, SYMBOL_ALREADY_DEFINED_ERROR, UNTERMINED_COMMENT_ERROR). keywords.c / .h Maps lowercase-normalized identifiers against Pascal reserved keywords (BEGIN..END) via iskeyword(). lexer.c / .h Implements skipspaces(), isID(), isNUM(), isASGN(), isRELOP(), and gettoken(), maintaining lexeme, linenum, and colnum. parser.c / .h Implements all \(\text{LL}(1)\) recursive descent procedures (program, block, vardef, sbprgdef, parmlist, beginend, stmtlst, stmt, expr, smpexpr, term, factor, type) and match(). symtab.c / .h Implements symtab_append(), symtab_lookup(), and formatted tabular inspection via symtab_print().

docs.title: 1. Multi-Level Lexical Scoping (inputs/relop.pas)
docs.text:
Executing ./mypas inputs/relop.pas parses a program containing three nested lexical levels (Global \(\rightarrow\) CompareValues \(\rightarrow\) CheckEqual / CheckGreaterOrEqual), printing intermediate symbol table states as each inner block exits and unwinding inner frames back to lexlevel = 1:

symtab after block:
#  | NAME                              | LEXLEVEL | OBJECT TYPE |   TYPE   | IS PARAM? 
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0  | input                             | 1        | variable    | text     | yes 
1  | output                            | 1        | variable    | text     | yes 
2  | x                                 | 1        | variable    | int32    | no 
3  | y                                 | 1        | variable    | int32    | no 
4  | CompareValues                     | 1        | procedure   | int32    | no 
5  | a                                 | 2        | variable    | int32    | yes

docs.title: MySh Command-Line Shell
docs.text:
Custom POSIX Command-Line Shell in C

A lightweight, POSIX-compliant interactive command-line interpreter implemented in C11 from first principles using UNIX system calls. Developed for the Operating Systems II (Sistemas Operacionais II) course at São Paulo State University (UNESP), MySh demonstrates kernel-level process lifecycle orchestration (fork, execvp, waitpid), unidirectional inter-process communication (pipe, dup2), asynchronous terminal signal isolation (SIGINT, SIGTSTP), and parent-process built-in state management (chdir).

docs.title: Quick Links
docs.text:

docs.title: System Architecture & REPL Execution Pipeline
docs.text:
MySh operates as an infinite Read–Eval–Print Loop (REPL) executing in user space while delegating process isolation, file-descriptor redirection, and binary loading directly to the OS kernel via POSIX system calls:

flowchart TD
    Prompt["🖥️ Dynamic Prompt Generator<br/>(build_prompt)<br/>[MySh] user@host:~/cwd$"] --> Read["⌨️ Input Stream Reader<br/>(fgets + newline strip)"]
    Read --> Builtin{"🔍 Built-in Command?<br/>(exit | cd | cd ~ | cd path)"}

    Builtin -->|"Yes (Parent Process)"| ParentExec["🏠 In-Process Execution<br/>chdir() / exit()"]
    ParentExec --> Prompt

    Builtin -->|"No (External Pipeline)"| Tokenizer["✂️ Pipeline Tokenizer<br/>(parse_args)<br/>Splits tokens on ' ' / '\\t' & '|'"]
    Tokenizer --> PipeSetup["🔗 Kernel Pipe Allocation<br/>pipe(fd) ➔ [fd[0] read, fd[1] write]"]
    PipeSetup --> Fork["🧬 Process Duplication<br/>pid = fork()"]

    Fork -->|"Child (pid == 0)"| ChildProc["👶 Child Process Setup<br/>1. Restore SIG_DFL<br/>2. dup2(input_fd, STDIN)<br/>3. dup2(fd[1], STDOUT)<br/>4. execvp(args[0], args)"]
    Fork -->|"Parent (pid > 0)"| ParentWait["⏳ Parent Synchronization<br/>1. Close unused FDs<br/>2. Pass fd[0] to next stage<br/>3. waitpid(pid, &status, 0)"]

    ParentWait --> Prompt

docs.title: Core Operating Systems Invariants
docs.text:
1. Parent vs. Child State Separation: State-mutating shell built-ins (cd, exit) must execute inside the parent shell process. Invoking chdir() inside a forked child would alter only the child's process control block (PCB) current working directory, leaving the parent shell's directory unchanged upon child termination.
  2. Strict File Descriptor Hygiene: Every open pipe endpoint (fd[0] and fd[1]) not actively bound to STDIN_FILENO (0) or STDOUT_FILENO (1) is closed immediately in both parent and child processes. Failing to close the write end (fd[1]) in the parent prevents downstream consumers (e.g., grep, wc, sort) from receiving EOF (read() == 0), which would otherwise cause pipeline deadlocks.
  3. Cross-Platform POSIX Portability: Preprocessor guards provide fallback definitions for LOGIN_NAME_MAX, HOST_NAME_MAX, and PATH_MAX across Linux (glibc) and macOS/BSD (Darwin) toolchains.

docs.title: Kernel Mechanics & POSIX System Call Breakdown
1. Process Lifecycle & Image Replacement (fork, execvp, waitpid)
docs.text:
When executing an external binary (e.g., ls -la), MySh follows the classic UNIX fork–exec–wait pattern inside run_command():

  1. fork(): Clones the calling shell process, creating a child process with a distinct PID and a copy-on-write (CoW) replica of the parent's virtual address space and open file descriptor table.
  2. execvp(args[0], args): Replaces the child's entire memory image (.text, .data, .bss, heap, and stack) with the target executable resolved across the colon-delimited directories in the $PATH environment variable, preserving the redirected file descriptors 0, 1, and 2.
  3. waitpid(pid, &status, 0): Suspends the parent REPL until the foreground child terminates, reaping the child's exit status from the kernel process table to prevent zombie processes (Z state) and inspecting termination causes via WIFEXITED(status) and WIFSIGNALED(status).

docs.title: 2. Multi-Stage Pipeline Plumbing (pipe, dup2)
docs.text:
For arbitrary \(k\)-stage command pipelines (cmd_1 | cmd_2 | ... | cmd_k), parse_args() iterates through whitespace-delimited tokens and chains consecutive stages using unidirectional kernel ring buffers:

Pipeline Stage input_fd (STDIN_FILENO) has_next_pipe STDOUT_FILENO Target Parent Action After fork() Stage 1 (cmd_1) STDIN_FILENO (0) 1 (true) dup2(fd₁[1], 1) Closes fd₁[1]; stores next_input_fd = fd₁[0] Stage \(m\) (cmd_m) dup2(fdₘ₋₁[0], 0) 1 (true) dup2(fdₘ[1], 1) Closes fdₘ₋₁[0] and fdₘ[1]; updates next_input_fd = fdₘ[0] Stage \(k\) (cmd_k) dup2(fdₖ₋₁[0], 0) 0 (false) Terminal STDOUT_FILENO (1) Closes fdₖ₋₁[0]; awaits final exit status

docs.title: 3. Asynchronous Signal Isolation (SIGINT & SIGTSTP)
docs.text:
Interactive shells must remain resilient to keyboard-generated terminal signals sent to the foreground process group:

  • Parent Shell (main): Registers a no-op signal handler (ignore_signals) for SIGINT (Ctrl+C) and SIGTSTP (Ctrl+Z), ensuring accidental interrupt keystrokes do not terminate or suspend the active shell session.
  • Child Processes (pid == 0): Explicitly resets both handlers to kernel defaults (signal(SIGINT, SIG_DFL) and signal(SIGTSTP, SIG_DFL)) prior to calling execvp(), allowing users to interrupt or suspend long-running foreground commands (e.g., cat, sleep 30, ping) normally.

docs.title: 4. Context-Aware Prompt & Heap Safety (build_prompt)
docs.text:
Before each prompt render, build_prompt() queries user identity (getlogin_r with $USER fallback), network hostname (gethostname), and working directory (getcwd), substituting the $HOME prefix with ~ via memmove() to render:

[MySh] <username>@<hostname>:<abbreviated_cwd>$

The dynamically allocated prompt buffer is freed (free(prompt)) immediately after fflush(stdout) on every REPL cycle, maintaining zero heap memory leaks across long-running interactive sessions.

docs.title: Parallel Voronoi Diagram
docs.text:
Computational Geometry & Shared-Memory HPC

A high-performance C++ implementation of planar Voronoi tessellation built from first principles using half-plane intersection clipping and OpenMP shared-memory multithreading. Developed for the Parallel and Distributed Programming course at São Paulo State University (UNESP), the project explores both exact geometric construction and empirical concurrency trade-offs across sequential, outer-loop parallel, and nested-loop parallel execution models.

docs.title: Quick Links
docs.text:
• Source Code Repository: github.com/joaohb07/programacao-paralela-e-distribuida
  • Authors: João Henrique Botelho (201154048), João Vitor Figueredo (201154072), João Pedro Brum (201152428)
  • Course & Institution: Parallel and Distributed Programming — UNESP

docs.title: 1. Planar Voronoi Tessellation Definition
docs.text:
Given a finite set of \(n\) distinct generator sites \(S = \{p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n\} \subset \mathbb{R}^2\) bounded within a closed rectangular domain \(\Omega = [0, L] \times [0, L]\), the Voronoi cell \(V(p_i)\) associated with site \(p_i\) is the locus of all points in \(\Omega\) closer to \(p_i\) than to any other site \(p_j \in S \setminus \{p_i\}\) under the Euclidean metric \(d(x, y) = \|x - y\|_2\):

\[ V(p_i) = \left\{ x \in \Omega \;\middle|\; \|x - p_i\|_2 \le \|x - p_j\|_2, \;\forall j \neq i \right\} \]

Geometrically, each cell \(V(p_i)\) is a convex polygon formed by the intersection of the bounding box \(\Omega\) with \(n - 1\) closed half-planes:

\[ V(p_i) = \Omega \cap \bigcap_{j \neq i} H(p_i, p_j) \]

where \(H(p_i, p_j)\) denotes the half-plane containing \(p_i\) bounded by the perpendicular bisector \(B(p_i, p_j)\).

docs.title: 2. Analytical Half-Plane Clipping Pipeline
docs.text: Instead of relying on Fortune's sweep-line algorithm or Delaunay dualization, the implementation computes each cell independently via incremental convex polygon clipping (New_Cell), making every site's cell construction data-independent from all other sites:

docs.title: A. Perpendicular Bisector Line Equation (Get_Bisector)
docs.text:
For two generator sites \(A = (x_A, y_A)\) and \(B = (x_B, y_B)\), let \(M = \left(\frac{x_A + x_B}{2}, \frac{y_A + y_B}{2}\right)\) be their midpoint. The normal vector \(\vec{n} = B - A = (x_B - x_A, y_B - y_A)\) defines the implicit line equation \(ax + by + c = 0\):

\[ \begin{aligned} a &= x_B - x_A \\ b &= y_B - y_A \\ c &= -a \cdot \left(\frac{x_A + x_B}{2}\right) - b \cdot \left(\frac{y_A + y_B}{2}\right) \end{aligned} \]

docs.title: B. Line–Segment Intersection via Homogeneous Cross Product (intersec_Bi_Pnt)
docs.text:
Given a polygon edge \(\overline{UV}\) with endpoints \(U = (x_U, y_U)\) and \(V = (x_V, y_V)\), its supporting line coefficients \(\mathbf{v} = (v_0, v_1, v_2)\) are computed in homogeneous coordinates \(\mathbb{P}^2\):

\[ \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} y_U - y_V \\ x_V - x_U \\ x_U y_V - y_U x_V \end{pmatrix} \]

The intersection \(\mathbf{z} = (z_0, z_1, z_2)\) between the bisector \(\mathbf{b} = (a, b, c)\) and edge line \(\mathbf{v}\) is obtained via the 3D cross product \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{v}\):

\[ \mathbf{z} = \begin{pmatrix} b v_2 - c v_1 \\ c v_0 - a v_2 \\ a v_1 - b v_0 \end{pmatrix} \]
  • If \(z_2 = 0\), the bisector and polygon edge are parallel (no intersection).
  • Otherwise, the Cartesian intersection point is \(T = \left(\frac{z_0}{z_2}, \frac{z_1}{z_2}\right)\), validated against segment bounds via collinear distance check (Is_in_line): \(\|U - T\|_2 + \|V - T\|_2 \approx \|U - V\|_2\).

docs.title: C. Half-Plane Vertex Pruning & Angular Ordering
docs.text:
1. Out-of-Cell Vertex Removal: Any existing vertex \(W\) of cell \(V(p_i)\) whose segment \(\overline{Wp_i}\) intersects the bisector \(B(p_i, p_j)\) lies on the opposing half-plane \(H(p_j, p_i)\) and is pruned (dellist), while valid intersection points \(T\) are inserted into the polygon vertex list.
  2. Counter-Clockwise Polar Sorting (Sort_Points_Anti_Clockwise): Because vertex insertion disrupts cyclic edge adjacency, vertices are partitioned into lower (\(y \le y_p\)) and upper (\(y > y_p\)) half-planes relative to site \(p\) and sorted by polar angle using the dot-product law of cosines:
\[ \theta = \arccos\left(\frac{\overrightarrow{PQ_1} \cdot \overrightarrow{PQ_2}}{\|\overrightarrow{PQ_1}\|_2 \, \|\overrightarrow{PQ_2}\|_2}\right) \cdot \frac{180}{\pi} \]

docs.title: Parallel Architecture & OpenMP Strategies
docs.text:
Because each Voronoi cell \(V(p_i)\) depends only on read-only access to the global point set \(S\) and iterative mutations to its own local polygon boundary, the outer loop over sites \(i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}\) exhibits embarrassingly parallel structure with \(\mathcal{O}(n^2)\) total arithmetic work across \(n\) sites.

flowchart TD
    Input["📍 Deterministic Grid Generator<br/>pointgen(boxsize, gridsize)<br/>N = (boxsize / gridsize)² sites"] --> Fork["⚡ #pragma omp parallel for<br/>(Thread Team Spawned)"]

    subgraph ThreadWork ["Thread-Local Execution (Zero Shared-State Mutation)"]
        direction TB
        T1["🧵 Thread 0<br/>Site p₀ ➔ Private local_cell<br/>Clip against q₁..qₙ + Polar Sort"]
        T2["🧵 Thread 1<br/>Site p₁ ➔ Private local_cell<br/>Clip against q₁..qₙ + Polar Sort"]
        TK["🧵 Thread k<br/>Site pᵢ ➔ Private local_cell<br/>Clip against q₁..qₙ + Polar Sort"]
    end

    Fork --> T1
    Fork --> T2
    Fork --> TK

    T1 --> Crit["🔒 #pragma omp critical<br/>cells.push_back(local_cell)"]
    T2 --> Crit
    TK --> Crit

    Crit --> Result["📐 Complete Voronoi Tessellation<br/>std::deque<Cell> cells"]

docs.title: Comparative Analysis of Implemented Variants
docs.text:
The repository implements and benchmarks three execution models to evaluate synchronization overhead, thread contention, and data-race hazards:

Implementation Parallelization Strategy Synchronization & Memory Model Architectural Assessment sequential.cpp Single-threaded baseline (\(1\) core) Reuses a single mutable Cell struct reset after each site \(p_i\). Baseline (\(\mathcal{O}(n^2)\)): Zero thread overhead; establishes reference wall-clock runtime. parallel_voronoi_1.cpp Coarse-grained outer-loop parallelism (#pragma omp parallel for on loop \(i\)) Each thread instantiates a stack-private Cell local_cell = cell, avoiding false sharing during clipping, and synchronizes once at completion via #pragma omp critical. Optimal Strategy: Maximizes computation-to-synchronization ratio. Threads execute all \(n-1\) bisector clips and polar sorts independently in private memory. parallel_voronoi_2.cpp Nested loop parallelism (#pragma omp parallel for on both outer loop \(i\) and inner loop \(j\)) Inner threads concurrently read and overwrite local_cell.listpoints = New_Cell(...) without mutual exclusion. Anti-Pattern / Hazard: Introduces severe thread-spawning overhead at every site \(p_i\) and a data race on local_cell.listpoints because sequential half-plane clipping is inherently loop-carried across \(j\).

Key Concurrency Insight: In convex polygon clipping, iteration \(j+1\) requires the exact vertex polygon produced by iteration \(j\) (\(V^{(j+1)}(p_i) = V^{(j)}(p_i) \cap H(p_i, q_{j+1})\)). Consequently, the inner loop \(j\) carries a true flow dependency (RAW hazard), proving why coarse-grained outer-loop decomposition (parallel_voronoi_1.cpp) is both mathematically sound and faster.

docs.text:

docs.title: Performance Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Consistent \(\sim 64\%\) Latency Reduction: Across both problem sizes (\(400\) and \(576\) sites), parallel_voronoi_1.cpp cuts wall-clock execution time by nearly two-thirds compared to sequential.cpp.
  2. Amdahl's Law & Critical Section Amortization: Because each thread performs \(\mathcal{O}(n)\) polygon clipping and sorting steps before acquiring #pragma omp critical once to append local_cell to std::deque<Cell>, lock contention remains negligible even as \(N\) scales up.

docs.title: Wireless Sensor Network Optimization
docs.text:
Minimum Spanning Tree (Kruskal vs. Prim)

A graph-theoretic combinatorial optimization framework in Python designed to minimize physical cabling infrastructure, deployment cost, and transmission latency across geographically distributed Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs). Developed for the Graph Theory (Teoria dos Grafos) course at São Paulo State University (UNESP), the project models planar sensor topologies as weighted complete graphs and implements both Kruskal's and Prim's Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) algorithms from scratch, accompanied by step-by-step trace diagnostics, Matplotlib topology rendering, and a pytest automated unit test suite.

docs.title: System Architecture & Optimization Pipeline
docs.text:
The codebase follows a clean object-oriented separation of concerns across domain entities (Sensor), graph data structures and greedy MST solvers (Graph), and visualization/telemetry utilities (Helpers):

flowchart TD
    CSV["📄 Spatial Sensor Datasets<br/>(data/sensores20..60.csv)<br/>Node ID, Type, (x, y)"] --> CLI["🖥️ Interactive CLI Selector<br/>(main.py)<br/>Dynamic Dataset Discovery"]
    CLI --> Model["🌐 Complete Graph Builder<br/>(Graph.build_graph)<br/>n(n−1)/2 Euclidean Edges"]
    Model --> PlotOrig["📊 Full Topology Plot<br/>(Helpers.plot_graph)"]

    Model --> Kruskal["🌲 Kruskal's MST Solver<br/>(Graph.kruskal)<br/>Edge Sort + Component Union"]
    Model --> Prim["🌿 Prim's MST Solver<br/>(Graph.prim)<br/>Cut-Property Frontier Expansion"]

    Kruskal --> Verify["✅ Optimality & Cost Verification<br/>Total Cost = ∑ w(e) (Exact Parity)<br/>+ Matplotlib MST Rendering + Pytest"]
    Prim --> Verify

docs.title: Core Engineering Invariants
docs.text:
1. Exact Global Optimum Parity: Because all edge weights represent distinct or metric Euclidean distances in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), both greedy algorithms are mathematically guaranteed by the Cut Property and Cycle Property of matroids/graphs to converge to the exact same minimum total cable length \(W(T^*) = \sum_{e \in T^*} w(e)\) containing \(|V| - 1\) edges.
  2. Modular Domain Decomposition: Algorithmic logic (Grafo.py, Sensor.py) is strictly decoupled from I/O and plotting side effects (Helpers.py), enabling headless unit testing via pytest and unittest.mock.
  3. Multi-Scale Dataset Benchmarking: Includes five spatial sensor benchmarks (sensores20.csv, sensores25.csv, sensores34.csv, sensores45.csv, and sensores60.csv) to evaluate spanning tree behavior across varying node densities (\(|V| \in [20, 60]\)).

docs.title: 1. Planar Euclidean Graph Model (Graph.build_graph)
docs.text:
Let \(V = \{v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n\}\) denote the set of \(n\) spatial sensor nodes and central base station, where each vertex \(v_i\) is embedded in the Euclidean plane at coordinates \((x_i, y_i) \in \mathbb{R}^2\).

The network topology is modeled as an undirected, weighted complete graph \(G = (V, E)\) with \(|V| = n\) vertices and \(|E| = \binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}\) candidate links, where the edge weight function \(w: E \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}\) measures the Euclidean cable length between sensors \(v_i\) and \(v_j\):

\[ w(v_i, v_j) = \Vert{}v_i - v_j\Vert{}_2 = \sqrt{(x_i - x_j)^2 + (y_i - y_j)^2} \]

docs.title: 2. Minimum Spanning Tree Objective
docs.text:
We seek an acyclic connected subgraph (spanning tree) \(T = (V, E_T)\) with \(E_T \subseteq E\) and \(|E_T| = |V| - 1\) that minimizes total infrastructure length:

\[ \min_{T \subseteq G} W(T) = \sum_{e \in E_T} w(e) \quad \text{subject to } T \text{ spanning all } v \in V \text{ without cycles.} \]

docs.title: 1. Kruskal's Algorithm (Graph.kruskal) — Edge-Centric Greedy Selection
docs.text:
Kruskal's algorithm constructs the MST globally by sorting all \(|E|\) candidate edges in non-decreasing order of Euclidean weight and iteratively adding the lightest edge that connects two disjoint connected components:

  1. Global Edge Sorting: Sorts self.edges in ascending order of \(w(e)\) in \(\mathcal{O}(|E| \log |E|)\) time.
  2. Acyclic Component Merging: Maintains a component representative dictionary parent[node.node] initialized to each node's own identifier. For each edge \((u, v, w)\):
  3. If parent[u] != parent[v], the edge does not induce a cycle; it is appended to mst, total_cost is incremented by \(w\), and all vertices sharing old_parent are merged into new_parent.
  4. Otherwise, the edge is discarded.
  5. Step-by-Step Telemetry: Logs each accepted link (u - v), edge weight, and cumulative cost via Helpers.print_mst_step_by_step().

docs.title: 2. Prim's Algorithm (Graph.prim) — Vertex-Centric Frontier Expansion
docs.text:
Prim's algorithm grows a single connected tree outward from an arbitrary root node (start_node = self.nodes[0]) by repeatedly selecting the minimum-weight edge crossing the cut \((S, V \setminus S)\) between visited_nodes (\(S\)) and unvisited_nodes (\(V \setminus S\)):

  1. Initialization: Sets \(S = \{v_0\}\) and \(U = V \setminus \{v_0\}\) (represented as Python hash sets visited_nodes and unvisited_nodes).
  2. Cut-Edge Selection: While \(U \neq \emptyset\), scans candidate edges incident to \(S\) with at least one endpoint in \(U\), selecting nearest_edge with minimum Euclidean distance.
  3. Tree Expansion: Appends nearest_edge to mst, moves the newly reached endpoint(s) from unvisited_nodes to visited_nodes, and accumulates total_cost.

docs.text:
The application runs as a decoupled, multi-container service inside a private Ubuntu home-lab environment, isolated across dedicated Docker bridge networks and securely exposed to the internet without opening router ports (bypassing CGNAT).

flowchart TD
    Client["🌐 Browser / Client<br/>(HTTPS Request)"] --> Funnel["🔒 Tailscale Funnel<br/>(TLS Termination :443)"]
    Funnel --> NPM["🔀 Nginx Proxy Manager<br/>(Reverse Proxy :80)"]

        subgraph AppRuntime ["global-proxy + task-net"]
            Express["⚡ Express REST API<br/>(/api/*)"]
            Static["📦 Vue 3 + Carbon SPA<br/>(client/dist)"]

        end

docs.title: Key Architectural Decisions
docs.text:
1. Dual-Network Container Isolation (global-proxy vs. task-net):
  2. The task-app container attaches to both the shared global-proxy network (for reverse proxy ingress) and an isolated internal bridge network (task-net).
  3. The task-mongo database container attaches exclusively to task-net with no host ports exposed, preventing external or cross-project network access to the database layer.
  4. Unified Single-Origin Deployment (Multi-Stage Docker):
  5. Stage 1 (frontend-builder): Compiles the Vue 3 + Vite + IBM Carbon bundle using relative asset resolution (base: './') into static assets (client/dist).
  6. Stage 2 (backend-builder): Installs lean production Node.js dependencies (npm ci --omit=dev).
  7. Stage 3 (runtime): Runs on node:22-alpine under a non-root user (USER node), serving both the /api REST endpoints and the compiled SPA from a single origin on port 3000 — eliminating CORS overhead.
  8. Subpath Reverse Proxy Routing:
  9. Hosted under /task-app/ via Nginx Proxy Manager, stripping the path prefix before forwarding requests to http://task-app:3000. Relative API paths in Axios (baseURL: './api') and hash-based client routing (createWebHashHistory()) ensure seamless operation across both root (localhost) and subpath (/task-app/) environments.
  10. Zero-Trust Edge Ingress:
  11. Tailscale Funnel handles public DNS and automatic SSL/TLS certificate termination at the edge, forwarding clean HTTP traffic to Nginx without exposing the server's residential IP.

docs.title: Key Architectural Decisions
docs.text:
1. Unified Single-Origin Deployment (Multi-Stage Docker): Instead of maintaining separate containers for frontend and backend (which introduces CORS overhead and network latency), the Dockerfile executes a 3-stage pipeline:
  2. Stage 1 (frontend-builder): Compiles the React + Vite + Tailwind bundle with relative asset resolution (base: './') into static assets (client/dist).
  3. Stage 2 (backend-builder): Installs lean production-only Node.js dependencies (npm ci --omit=dev).
  4. Stage 3 (runtime): Runs under a non-root node user on node:22-alpine, where Express serves both the /weather REST endpoint and the static SPA on port 3000.
  5. Subpath Reverse Proxy Routing: Hosted under the /weather-app/ subpath via Nginx Proxy Manager over an internal Docker bridge network (global-proxy). Path-stripping rules and relative Vite asset paths ensure seamless routing alongside other hosted services on the same domain.
  6. Zero-Trust Edge Ingress: External traffic is routed through Tailscale Funnel, handling automatic SSL/TLS termination at the edge and forwarding clean HTTP traffic to the internal reverse proxy.

docs.title: Backend & API Orchestration
docs.text:
• Node.js (v22) & Express: Lightweight, event-driven HTTP server exposing a unified /weather endpoint that orchestrates sequential external API calls (Geocode ➔ Forecast) with structured error handling and query sanitization.
  • OpenCage Data API: Converts unstructured location queries (city names, addresses, landmarks) into standardized geographic coordinates (latitude, longitude, formatted location name).
  • OpenWeather Map API: Retrieves real-time meteorological telemetry (temperature, feels-like, humidity, wind speed, weather conditions) supporting dynamic localization (lang=en / lang=pt).

docs.title: Frontend & Data Visualization
docs.text:
• React & Vite: Fast Single-Page Application (SPA) with component-driven architecture and development proxy forwarding (/weather ➔ localhost:3000).
  • Tailwind CSS: Utility-first responsive styling engineered for clean visual hierarchy across desktop and mobile viewports.
  • d3-geo: Renders interactive geographic map projections centered dynamically on the searched coordinates.
  • i18next (react-i18next): Client-side internationalization engine seamlessly toggling UI labels and API weather descriptions between English and Portuguese.

docs.title: Quality Assurance & Automated Testing
docs.text:
• Jest & Supertest: Backend unit and HTTP integration tests validating API response contracts, query parameter validation (400 Bad Request on missing/invalid locations), and external service mocks.
  • Cypress: Automated End-to-End (E2E) and component testing verifying user search flows, language switching, and UI state transitions against a running application instance.

docs.text:
The confectionery “Confeita & Ria” hired you to program a new weekly ordering system. Since their budget is incredibly low, briefly consider that:

  • There are only two types of products for sale: cakes and juices;
  • An order consists of 1 to 2 the same or different products;
  • There is space to store only 2 products PER ORDER;
  • There is space to register only 3 requests PER DAY;
  • There is space to store orders only for 7 days (Sun to Sat).

docs.title: Products
docs.text:
Every product has the following information in common:

  • value: decimal
  • In addition, each product may have unique characteristics, that is, that only it implements.

Cake is a product with:

  • Flavor
  • Orange (constant: 1);
  • Apple (constant: 2);
  • Cover:char (may or may not have cover) ('s'/'n').

Juice is a product with:

  • Flavor
  • Orange (constant: 1);
  • Apple (constant: 2);

docs.title: Orders
docs.text:
Each order stores the following information:

  • order_id:integer (auto-increment) (starting with 1);
  • qty_products:integer (stores the quantity of products in this order)

  • products:product[2] (each order can have up to 2 products);

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Used an array of orders of size [7][3] that will be responsible for storing your orders. Each row corresponds to a day of the week and each column corresponds to one of the maximum 3 orders that can be made on each day.

In addition to the matrix, it is necessary to use a vector of indices of size [7] that will be responsible for storing the number of orders on each day of the week.

Example: Position 0 of the vector stores the number of orders that were registered in row 0 of the matrix (in this case on Monday).

def min_max(array):
    n = len(array)-1
    if (n%2) == 0:

    while (i<n-1):

def quick_sort(array,low,high):
 
    #  auxiliary stack

    stack = [0] * (size)
 
    top = -1
 
    top = top + 1
    stack[top] = low
    top = top + 1
    stack[top] = high
 
    # Keep popping from stack while is not empty

        top = top - 1
        low = stack[top]
        top = top - 1

            stack[top] = low
            top = top + 1
            stack[top] = p - 1

        #  push right side to stack
        if p+1 < high:
            top = top + 1
            stack[top] = p + 1
            top = top + 1
            stack[top] = high

docs.title: Stroke Prediction¶
docs.text:
Data Analysis & Classification

Practical Exploratory Data Analysis and Supervised Machine Learning project developed in Python to investigate clinical and demographic risk factors associated with Stroke occurrence, comparing the performance and hyperparameter sensitivity of different classifiers.

docs.title: Project Overview¶
docs.text: The goal of this notebook is to build a complete binary classification pipeline from the healthcare-dataset-stroke-data.csv dataset (\(5,110\) patient records), covering data cleaning and feature transformation through model training, hyperparameter tuning, and comparative evaluation across three distinct families of predictive models.

docs.title: Key Workflow Stages¶
docs.text:
1. Data Cleaning & Preprocessing (Pandas & Scikit-Learn):

    • Data type inspection, missing value identification (bmi containing \(201\) null records), and removal of discarded columns for modeling (id, bmi, and avg_glucose_level).
    • Standardization of the numerical feature age and cardinality analysis of categorical attributes (gender, ever_married, work_type, Residence_type, and smoking_status).
    • Encoding of qualitative variables using LabelEncoder followed by OneHotEncoder (ColumnTransformer), expanding the feature matrix to \(19\) features.
    • Standard normal (\(z\)-score) scaling with StandardScaler and stratified splitting into training (\(85\%\)) and testing (\(15\%\)) sets.

  2. Exploratory Analysis & Correlation (Seaborn & Matplotlib):

    • Generation of a correlation heatmap using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient to evaluate monotonic relationships between age, hypertension, heart disease history, and the target variable (stroke).

  3. Comparative Modeling & Hyperparameter Tuning:

    • Logistic Regression (LogisticRegression): Baseline evaluation using a confusion matrix (Yellowbrick) and experimentation across \(6\) combinations of penalties (l1, l2, elasticnet, none) and solvers (newton-cg, saga, sag, liblinear), achieving \(94.65\%\) accuracy.
    • Artificial Neural Network (MLPClassifier): Comparative experiments across optimizers (sgd with constant or invscaling learning rates, with and without Nesterov momentum, and adam), tracked via training loss curves over epochs, reaching up to \(94.65\%\) accuracy.
    • Linear Discriminant Analysis (LinearDiscriminantAnalysis): Comparison between svd and lsqr solvers across multiple regularization factors (shrinkage: auto, 0.1, 0.75), achieving a peak accuracy of \(93.61\%\).

docs.title: Architecture & Key Concepts
docs.text: Core networking, reverse-proxy routing, Zero-Trust tunneling, and operational automation powering the self-hosted jhbserver home-lab infrastructure.

docs.title: 1. Reverse Proxy & Proxy Hosts
docs.text:
A Reverse Proxy sits in front of one or more backend servers and intercepts incoming client requests before forwarding them to the appropriate internal service. Unlike a forward proxy (which hides the client's identity from external servers), a reverse proxy abstracts internal infrastructure topology from external clients:

  • Single Entry Point: Clients connect solely to a single public endpoint (https://jhbserver.tail4bcb71.ts.net), unaware of internal container names, private IP addresses, or internal ports (3000, 81, 27017).
  • Proxy Hosts: Logical virtual-host definitions inside Nginx Proxy Manager (NPM) that map incoming domain names (jhbserver.tail4bcb71.ts.net) to internal upstream targets (status-monitor:3000).
  • Subpath Routing & Prefix Stripping: Using NPM Custom Locations, multiple independent web applications share one domain without port conflicts. Appending a trailing slash / to both the Location (/task-app/) and the Forward Hostname (http://task-app/:3000) instructs Nginx to strip the /task-app prefix before passing the request to the upstream Express server:
Client Request:  GET https://jhbserver.tail4bcb71.ts.net/task-app/api/tasks
                                                       └───────┘ stripped by NPM
Upstream Target: GET http://task-app:3000/api/tasks

docs.title: 2. Tailscale Funnel (Zero-Trust Edge & TLS Termination)
docs.text:
Traditional self-hosting requires configuring Port Forwarding (80/443) on a residential router, managing Dynamic DNS (DDNS) for changing ISP IP addresses, and provisioning Let's Encrypt certificates via ACME challenges—which often fails behind carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT).

Tailscale Funnel solves this at the network edge: * Outbound Encrypted Tunnel: The tailscaled daemon on the Ubuntu host establishes an outbound WireGuard-encrypted connection to Tailscale's edge relays—zero inbound firewall ports need to be opened on the home router. * Automatic TLS Termination: Tailscale automatically provisions and renews valid TLS certificates for jhbserver.tail4bcb71.ts.net, terminating HTTPS (443/tcp) at the edge and forwarding plain HTTP traffic locally to 127.0.0.1:80 (Nginx Proxy Manager). * Private Administrative Plane: While public web routes are served via Funnel, administrative SSH (22/tcp) and the NPM dashboard (81/tcp) remain strictly restricted to the private LAN (192.168.0.0/24) and authenticated Tailscale VPN peers.

docs.title: 3. Container Hardening & Read-Only Socket Telemetry
docs.text: Exposing the Docker daemon socket (/var/run/docker.sock) with write permissions grants effective root control over the host machine. To observe container states safely without elevating privileges: * Read-Only Mount (:ro): status-monitor mounts /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro, restricting API calls strictly to GET inspection endpoints. * Least-Privilege Runtime: The container runs as the unprivileged node user (USER node), inherits the host docker group GID (group_add: ["977"]) solely for socket read access, enforces no-new-privileges:true, and locks its root filesystem (read_only: true).

docs.title: Operational Automation: Full-Stack Recovery Script
docs.text: When applying host kernel updates, recovering from power events, or refreshing reverse-proxy DNS bindings across containers, ~/server/scripts/restart-stack.sh deterministically restarts the ingress layer first and then brings up every containerized project.

docs.title: Script Source (~/server/scripts/restart-stack.sh)
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e

echo "=== Reiniciando Nginx Proxy Manager ==="
cd ~/server/proxy && docker compose up -d --force-recreate

echo "=== Reiniciando Aplicações ==="
for app in ~/server/projects/*; do
  if [ -f "$app/docker-compose.yml" ]; then
    echo "-> Subindo $(basename "$app")..."
    (cd "$app" && docker compose up -d)
  fi
done

echo "=== Status Atual ==="
docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}"

docs.title: How It Works Step-by-Step
docs.text: Step Command / Construct Purpose & Engineering Behavior 1. Fail-Fast Guard set -e Immediately aborts execution if any command exits with a non-zero status, preventing cascading failures if the proxy layer fails to start. 2. Ingress Recreation cd ~/server/proxy && docker compose up -d --force-recreate Recreates the nginx-proxy-manager container first so the global-proxy bridge gateway and internal DNS resolver are guaranteed to be active. 3. Project Discovery Loop for app in ~/server/projects/*; do ... done Dynamically iterates through every project folder (status-monitor, task-app, weather-app) without hardcoding paths—new projects are automatically included as soon as they are cloned. 4. Subshell Isolation (cd "$app" && docker compose up -d) Executes each docker compose up -d inside a subshell (...) so directory changes remain isolated per iteration without affecting the parent script's working directory. 5. Verification Table docker ps --format "table ..." Outputs a clean summary table showing container names, uptime/health statuses, and bound host ports to confirm zero unintended port exposure.

docs.title: Why Docker Compose Instead of Kubernetes?
docs.text: For a single-node home-lab, running Kubernetes (k3s or MicroK8s) introduces significant RAM/CPU overhead just to sustain the control plane, alongside unnecessary complexity around CNI networking and persistent volume provisioning. Docker Compose paired with segmented bridge networks and Nginx Proxy Manager delivers declarative service orchestration, automatic container recovery (restart: unless-stopped), and near-zero resource overhead.

  • Shared Ingress Bridge (global-proxy): Only web-facing containers attach to global-proxy. Because Nginx Proxy Manager resolves containers by service name over internal Docker DNS, application containers never bind host ports (3000, 27017), eliminating port collisions.
  • Database Isolation (task-net): Stateful services like task-mongo run exclusively on private per-project bridge networks, remaining completely unreachable from the reverse proxy or external networks.

docs.title: Security & Hardening Layers
docs.text:
The host and container runtime follow a defense-in-depth posture tailored for internet-exposed self-hosting:

  1. Host Firewall (UFW): Default incoming policy set to deny. Only local LAN (192.168.0.0/24) access to SSH (22/tcp) and the NPM admin UI (81/tcp), plus VPN traffic on tailscale0, are permitted. Public ingress flows exclusively through the Tailscale Funnel interface.
  2. SSH Hardening (sshd): Remote root login and password authentication are completely disabled (PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no), enforcing Ed25519 key-based authentication for both administrative sessions and GitHub Actions CD runners.
  3. Unprivileged Container Execution: Application images run under the restricted non-root node user (USER node) with no-new-privileges:true.
  4. Read-Only Docker Socket & Filesystem: The status-monitor service mounts /var/run/docker.sock strictly as read-only (:ro) alongside a read-only root filesystem (read_only: true), preventing container mutation or daemon write access even if compromised.
  5. Automated Patch Management: unattended-upgrades automatically applies critical kernel and OS security patches.

docs.text:
The status-monitor service aggregates host, storage, GPU, container, CI/CD, and network metrics without elevated container privileges (read_only: true, non-root node user):

Metric Source Collection Mechanism Data Exposed Host Kernel (os, fs & /sys) Native Node.js os, fs.statfsSync('/') & /sys/class/thermal Load averages (1m/5m/15m), DDR4 RAM usage, root filesystem capacity, uptime, CPU temperature In-Memory Ring Buffer 60-sample circular array (5s interval = 5-min window) Time-series history for client-side <svg> sparkline rendering NVIDIA GPU (nvidia-smi) Host systemd daemon exporting CSV to /run/gpu-telemetry.json (:ro) GPU model, core utilization (%), VRAM used/total (MB), GPU temperature (°C) Docker Engine API /containers/json + /containers/{id}/stats?stream=false over /var/run/docker.sock:ro Running containers, image tags, health states, per-container CPU % and active RAM (MB) GitHub Actions API Cached GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/deploy.yml/runs (60s TTL) Latest workflow conclusion (Passing / Failed) and short commit SHA Internal Bridge Probes Parallel fetch + AbortController (3s timeout) on global-proxy HTTP status codes and internal container-to-container latency (ms)

docs.title: How Telemetry Collection & Security Work
docs.text:
Instead of running heavyweight agents (like Prometheus or Grafana) or granting root privileges to containers, the status-monitor service collects real-time metrics using a zero-overhead, least-privilege design:

  • Client-Side Polling & CORS: Because this documentation site is statically hosted on GitHub Pages (https://joaohb07.github.io), the Express backend enables read-only CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, GET only) on /api/status, allowing the browser to poll fresh metrics every 5 seconds directly over the Tailscale Funnel HTTPS endpoint.
  • Read-Only Host & Container Access: The container runs with a read-only root filesystem (read_only: true) under a non-root node user. It queries Docker engine state and cgroup stats via raw HTTP requests over /var/run/docker.sock:ro and reads GPU metrics from an atomic file (/run/gpu-telemetry.json:ro) exported every 5 seconds by a host systemd unit running nvidia-smi.
  • Rate-Limit-Safe CI/CD Status & Ring Buffer: Historical sparklines are served from an in-memory 60-point circular buffer without external databases, while GitHub Actions workflow runs are cached in memory for 60 seconds to prevent upstream API rate limiting.
  • Internal Network Probing: Latency measurements (latencyMs) reflect true container-to-container response times inside the isolated global-proxy Docker bridge network, bypassing public DNS and TLS overhead.
